chapter_theme: Under the heading ஊழ், fourteen verses argue that fate rules effort, understanding, guarding, service to kings and escape: what is due befalls the highest and the unwilling, gain falls to those whose earlier good deeds or penance earned it, the fortunate have no evil day, the foe is only the agent of one's old deed, and survivors of fire come to escape or to rule.

227.reading: The verse asks what diligent effort, which reaches its goal with hardship as its companion, can do once the deity has settled the outcome, addressing the lord of a town where bees swarm and hum at the blossoms, and closes with a proverb that digging a set pit is of no use where the kurumbu moves.
227.nuance: The question is rhetorical and grants effort its full credit first (எவ்வம் துணையாய்ப் பொருள்முடிக்கும்) before denying it any force against தெய்வம். The proverb's terms are hard: குறும்பு may be a marauding band or a wild creature and கோப்புக் குழி a pit laid out as a trap, so the sense would be that a prepared trap is idle where the quarry goes its own way; this is a guess.

pazhamozhi.literal: where the kurumbu moves about, there is no making of a laid-out pit

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to anyone whose effort meets an outcome the deity has fixed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort, however hard, cannot prevail where the deity has already settled the end

228.reading: Even in men of great understanding, pointed out by name, when many contrary turns befall them, their undertakings go after the kind of the fortune that has fallen to them, and so, the proverb says, fate defeats understanding.
228.nuance: The claim is about outcomes (கருமம்), not about the wise man's judgment going bad: his knowledge is intact and still loses. பொறி here is the mark of fortune, the word the Kural uses in 618.

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to renowned wise men whose works miscarry

pazhamozhi.applied_to: understanding, however great, does not secure the outcome of a man's works

229.reading: Even the moon, which spreads its broad light across the beautiful sky, is seen to come to harm, the verse tells the lord of the beautiful hill country where falls leap onto the rocks, and so what is bound to befall befalls everyone.
229.nuance: The moon is the instance, not an ornament: if the brightest and highest thing suffers its waning or its seizure, no rank exempts a person. தீங்குறுதல் does not say which harm, waning or eclipse.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is due to befall befalls anyone

story.act: no story; the moon's harm is the instance, and the proverb is applied to everyone

pazhamozhi.applied_to: no height or brightness exempts anyone from what is bound to befall

230.reading: Because the elephant tied up at Kazhumalam went to the excellent man of Karuvur, the verse says, whether one wants excellent things or does not want them, it is hard for what is bound to befall to pass without touching one.
230.nuance: The proverb line is almost word for word the last line of Naladiyar 109 (உற்றபால there, உறற்பால here), so the verse proves its point with a known saying; but where the Naladiyar speaks of unwanted evil, the elephant story turns it to unsought good. The episode is only alluded to: the verse names two places and an elephant that went to a man, and does not say that he was made king.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is bound to befall can hardly be kept from touching one

story.act: an elephant tied at Kazhumalam went to an excellent man of Karuvur
story.tradition: good fortune comes to the one it is due to, whether he seeks it or not

pazhamozhi.applied_to: by tradition the elephant sent out to choose a king, which chose a man of Karuvur; the verse names only the elephant, the two places and the man

231.reading: Though one guard all night, shouting, the tall fine palmyra that has grown up, its fruit falls only to those it is to fall to, and fortune too, the proverb says, touches only those it is to touch.
231.nuance: The image sets the watchman who stays up crying out against the one the fruit happens to drop to, so guarding is shown not to confer the gain. The lengthened forms (ஆஅய், ஏஎய், வாஅய்) are metrical.

pazhamozhi.literal: fortune too touches those it is due to touch

story.act: a man guards a tall palmyra all night and its fruit still falls to another

pazhamozhi.applied_to: gain goes to the one fated for it, not to the one who guards it

232.reading: Can those who did not do great good deeds earlier, without fail, get great wealth later, and what comes of setting out to make wealth by vying with those who have stores, the verse asks, since for those with no capital there is no profit.
232.nuance: The proverb is a merchant's rule, and the verse makes earlier good deeds the capital, so present striving is trade without principal. வைப்போடு இகலி is unclear: it may be rivalry with those who hold stored wealth, or striving against what is laid up by fate.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no profit for those without capital

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who seek great wealth without earlier good deeds

pazhamozhi.applied_to: without the capital of earlier good deeds, effort for wealth yields nothing

233.reading: Because the kani-vengai, though it has stood in its place for many days, blossoms only on the good day it seeks out, so wealth, even for those who serve kings so as to please them, gathers only at the time it is due to gather.
233.nuance: கணிவேங்கை is the vengai whose flowering marks the auspicious time, so the tree is itself a reckoner of days; the courtier's service is likened to its long standing, which does not make it bloom early.

pazhamozhi.literal: what is due to gather gathers at its time

story.act: no story; the vengai's timed flowering is the instance, applied to those who serve kings

pazhamozhi.applied_to: service to kings does not hasten wealth before its due time

234.reading: Those seized amid clamour, who have suffered the fault of capture, may yet break out and get away, the verse says, for the five who were free of falsehood escaped from the lac house, and there is no place without escape for those who are to escape.
234.nuance: The first line is obscure: குரைத்துக் கொளப்பட்டார் may be men denounced and taken, and கோளிழுக்கு the disgrace of capture. பொய்யற்ற gives the five a moral quality, but the proverb rests the escape on what is due, not on their truth.

pazhamozhi.literal: for one who is to escape there is no place he cannot escape from

story.act: the five free of falsehood got out of the lac house
story.tradition: those due to survive escape even from the surest trap

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the five of the lac house are, by tradition, the Pandavas of the Bharata story; the verse does not name them

235.reading: For those who are to prosper, even what was agreed to be surely bad turns out surely good, the verse tells the lord of the cool shore where flowers rich with honey give scent by the spreading waves, since for those who have fortune there is no evil day.
235.nuance: The proverb answers the reckoning of days: the bad day itself loses its force for one with திரு. ஆவார்க்கு, 'for those who will be', makes the good turn depend on the person's lot, not on the thing.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no evil day for those who have fortune

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those whose lot is to prosper

pazhamozhi.applied_to: for the fortunate even what all judged bad turns out good

236.reading: Even for those who have come to a king able to give, things do not come to hand, though wanted, except by the way of their lot, so one need not call them dull or small, since for those who did penance curry falls even into their rice.
236.nuance: The verse defends the unrewarded petitioner against contempt: his failure is his lot, not his want of sense. வீற்று வழி is not clear; it may be 'a separate way', the path one's own fortune opens. The proverb pictures gain falling of itself into the plate of one whose penance earned it.
236.domain_note: petitioners and dependants at a king's court

pazhamozhi.literal: for those who did penance the curry falls even into the rice

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who gain at court by the merit of earlier penance

pazhamozhi.applied_to: what a king gives reaches those whose earlier penance earned it, and the rest are not to be scorned

237.reading: For those whose time is to prosper even effort is not needed, and for those whose fortune is to leave, striving is fruitless, the verse tells the lord of the rocky hill country, so whatever one does and whatever one gets, for those not due to prosper nothing prospers.
237.nuance: The verse names ஆள்வினை and denies it on both sides: needless for the fortunate, useless for the unfortunate. ஆகும் சமயத்தார் makes the favourable lot a matter of timing.

pazhamozhi.literal: for those not due to prosper nothing comes to good

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those whose lot is against them

pazhamozhi.applied_to: effort neither helps the fortunate nor saves the unfortunate

238.reading: Not knowing that the old deed done in anger long ago has come and is punishing them now, why do people rage at the foes who make them suffer, the verse asks a woman with a lightning waist, since the servant who is sent also burns a town.
238.nuance: The proverb makes the enemy a mere agent: a town burned on a king's order is burned by his servant, and anger at the servant mistakes the hand for the cause. பண்டுருத்துச் செய்த puts anger at the origin of the deed, so the verse answers anger with anger's own past fruit.

pazhamozhi.literal: a man under orders burns even a town

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to the foe who brings suffering as the agent of one's past deed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: anger at those who harm one is misplaced, since they carry out one's own old deed

239.reading: The Chola's son, who came through alive after being burned, got the great elephant's nape and at last made his flawless sceptre run, and so, the proverb says, there is no deed that those who keep their life cannot attain.
239.nuance: The proverb fits the heading obliquely: it is less about fate's fixity than about survival keeping every outcome open, though the verse's sequence (burned, saved, mounted, enthroned) implies a lot working itself out. பிடர்த்தலைப் பேரானைப் பெற்று may mean he was carried on the state elephant's neck as the chosen king.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no deed beyond those who keep their life

story.act: a Chola prince survived burning, mounted the great elephant and in the end ruled with a just sceptre
story.tradition: so long as one lives, even kingship from ruin is within reach

pazhamozhi.applied_to: identified by tradition as Karikalan and the burning of his prison; the verse names only the Chola's son

240.reading: When things greatly to be feared come, those who know what is to be done do not fear their own distress, the verse tells the lord of the bamboo-ringed hill where the bull elephant, fearing the cold, embraces its mate, and the proverb sets this on ground where fate's arrow does not fall.
240.nuance: The closing proverb is elliptical: it may say the knowing stand as if on ground where fate's arrow cannot fall, or, read as an implied question, that there is no such ground and so fear is idle. The elephant sheltering its mate from the cold may hint that the wise meet danger by acting, not by fearing.

pazhamozhi.literal: on ground where fate's arrow does not fall

story.act: no story; the proverb is applied to those who know what to do when danger comes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: those who know their course are not shaken by the fear of what fate brings

links.note: Kural 619 grants that the deity may deny the end but says effort still pays the wage of bodily strain; Pazhamozhi 227 asks what effort can do at all once the deity has settled the end.
links.teaches: Both start from the same concession, that தெய்வம் can deny the goal, and part over what is left: the Kural keeps a wage for effort, while Pazhamozhi leaves it nothing, so the pair locates the precise point where the two works divide on effort and fate.
links.list_adds: its proverb of a pit dug in vain makes effort's labour itself the loss, where the couplet saves that labour as a wage.

links.note: Naladiyar 108 says that when the knowing do blameworthy things it comes from their past deeds; Pazhamozhi 228 says the works of renowned wise men go by their fortune, so fate defeats understanding.
links.teaches: Together the two verses show fate overriding knowledge in two places, in the wise man's conduct (the Naladiyar) and in the outcome of his works (Pazhamozhi), so knowing what is right secures neither right action nor success.
links.list_adds: it moves the quatrain's moral puzzle to the success of undertakings and seals it with a proverb that sets fate against understanding outright.

links.note: Both proverbs turn on உறற்பால, what is bound to befall: 229 proves it by the moon's harm, 230 by an elephant that went to a man of Karuvur.
links.teaches: Read together the same word covers both directions of fate, harm that strikes the highest and good that finds a man who did not seek it, so உறற்பால in this chapter is neutral lot, not misfortune only.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 230's proverb repeats almost word for word Naladiyar 109's last line, that wanted or not what is bound to come can hardly be kept from touching one; the Naladiyar applies it to unwanted evil, Pazhamozhi to an elephant that went to a man of Karuvur.
links.teaches: The pair shows a saying shared between the two works, and that Pazhamozhi re-aims it: the quatrain's line is a warning that unwanted evil cannot be fended off, and the elephant story makes it a promise that unsought good cannot be missed.
links.list_adds: it takes the quatrain's closing line as a proverb and backs it with a named episode, turning a general warning into a story of fortune arriving.

links.note: Kural 376 says what is not one's own will not stay though guarded, nor what is one's own leave though thrown away; Pazhamozhi 231 shows a palmyra guarded all night whose fruit still falls to the one it is due to.
links.teaches: The pairing turns the couplet's abstract 'guard' into a watchman shouting through the night under a tree, and adds a second person the couplet lacks, the passer-by who gets the fruit, so the loss of the guarder is someone else's unearned gain.
links.list_adds: it gives the couplet a scene with two people, guard and receiver, so fate's allotment is seen as a transfer, not only a keeping or a losing.

links.note: Kural 463 says the wise do not undertake a deed that loses the capital for the sake of gain; Pazhamozhi 232 says those who did no great good deeds before cannot have great wealth later, for without capital there is no profit.
links.teaches: The same trader's logic of capital and profit is prudence in the Kural and fate in Pazhamozhi, where the capital is earlier good deeds, so the pair shows the merchant's rule being moved from a counsel about risk to an account of merit.
links.list_adds: its proverb replaces the couplet's money capital with good deeds done before, so the capital cannot be raised now by any present skill.

links.note: Naladiyar 93 says wealth gathers when its time to gather comes, whether one gives or withholds; Pazhamozhi 233 says the same of those who serve kings, by the vengai that flowers only on its day.
links.teaches: The quatrain uses the timing of wealth to remove the miser's excuse, and Pazhamozhi uses it to remove the courtier's hope, so the same rule frees the giver to give and tells the servant of kings his service cannot hasten his reward.
links.list_adds: it carries the quatrain's rule from the giver's house to the king's court and gives it the image of a tree that flowers only on the right day.

links.note: 234 says the five got out of the lac house because there is no place without escape for one due to escape; 239 says the Chola's son survived burning and came to rule, for nothing is beyond those who keep their life.
links.teaches: Both proverbs follow an escape from fire, one from the epic and one from Tamil royal memory, and the second carries the story past survival to kingship, so the chapter makes surviving the fire the first step of a fortune still unfolding.

links.note: Kural 375 says that in making wealth the favourable can turn bad and the unfavourable good; Pazhamozhi 235 says that for those who are to prosper even what was judged bad turns out good, for the fortunate have no evil day.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves it open which way a thing will turn, and Pazhamozhi decides it by the person: the same reversal runs only toward good for one with fortune, so the pair shows the couplet's instability resolved by whose lot it is.
links.list_adds: it makes the reversal depend on the person's fortune and ties it to the reckoning of good and bad days, which the couplet does not mention.

links.note: Kural 618 says lacking fortune is no one's disgrace; Pazhamozhi 236 says that men who reach a generous king and still get nothing are not to be called dull or small, since gain comes by one's lot.
links.teaches: The couplet's general absolution becomes a defence of a particular figure, the empty-handed petitioner at court, and the pair shows the Kural's line on blame used to protect a man from the court's contempt rather than to urge him to work.
links.list_adds: it places the couplet's point at a king's court and adds a proverb of earned luck, so the failure is ascribed to unearned penance, not only excused.

links.note: Naladiyar 31 shows those who did no penance before clinging to the outer door of a house, unable to enter; Pazhamozhi 236 says for those who did penance curry falls even into their rice.
links.teaches: The two verses give both ends of one belief about past penance and present food: one man shut out at the door looking in, the other finding food falling into his plate, so the pair draws the full scale between beggary and luck as the fruit of earlier penance.
links.list_adds: its proverb shows the reward side that the quatrain leaves implied, and sets it at a king's court rather than at a rich man's house.

links.note: Kural 620 says those who toil without flagging see even fate's back; Pazhamozhi 237 says effort is needless for the fortunate and fruitless for the unfortunate.
links.teaches: Both name ஆள்வினை and fate together and give opposite verdicts on the same contest, the Kural letting tireless labour outrun fate and Pazhamozhi denying labour any effect in either lot, on the plain reading of both.
links.list_adds: it splits people into two lots and denies effort a role in each, where the couplet speaks of the single toiler who prevails.

links.note: Kural 371 says the fate of gain produces tireless effort and the fate of loss produces sloth; Pazhamozhi 237 says the fortunate need no effort and the striving of the unfortunate is fruitless.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps effort as fate's instrument, while Pazhamozhi makes it idle on both sides, so the pair shows two ways of subordinating effort to fate: as its product, or as beside the point.
links.list_adds: it pairs the two lots as the couplet does but cuts effort loose from them, so the fortunate prosper without it and the unfortunate strive in vain.

links.note: Naladiyar 33 says the fool breaks down when the fruit of past deeds arrives, while those who see it as old desert are freed of confusion; Pazhamozhi 238 says those who do not see their suffering as their old deed rage at the foes who cause it.
links.teaches: The quatrain turns the knowledge of old deeds against grief, and Pazhamozhi turns it against anger at enemies, recasting the foe as a servant carrying out an order, so the same doctrine is shown ending both despair and revenge.
links.list_adds: its proverb of the servant who burns the town on orders gives the enemy a role, the agent of one's own deed, that the quatrain does not consider.

links.note: Porunaratruppadai says Karikalan received his inheritance while still in the womb; Pazhamozhi 239 tells of a Chola's son who survived burning, mounted the great elephant and in the end ruled justly, a prince tradition identifies as Karikalan.
links.teaches: If the traditional identification holds, the same accession is told once as a birthright fixed before birth and once as a survival against fire, and the pair shows the ethics work turning a praised royal memory into proof that a living man can still come to anything.
links.list_adds: it uses the heroic memory not to praise the king but as a proverb's evidence, so the Chola's rise becomes a general lesson about survival.

links.note: Naladiyar 110 says that since what was set at the start cannot change, there is no reason to grieve when ruin comes; Pazhamozhi 240 says those who know what is to be done do not fear their distress when fearful things come.
links.teaches: Both ask for calm before what fate brings, but the quatrain grounds it in the fixity of the lot while Pazhamozhi grounds it in knowing what to do, so the pair shows two routes to the same composure, resignation and readiness.
links.list_adds: it rests calm on knowing one's course of action, with an image of an elephant sheltering its mate, rather than on the quatrain's sum that cannot be altered.

source_issues: Verse 227: the proverb குறும்பியங்கும் கோப்புக் குழிச்செய்வ(து) இல் is obscure in its key words and may be corrupt.
Verse 230: the proverb line nearly repeats the last line of Naladiyar 109 (உற்றபால there, உறற்பால here).
